title: Northeast India: Meghalaya, Assam and Arunachal in Two Weeks
metaDescription: A practical Northeast India itinerary covering Meghalaya’s living root bridges, Kaziranga, Majuli and Arunachal — with permits, seasons and transport.
excerpt: Living root bridges, the world’s wettest villages, river islands and one-horned rhinos — and almost no crowds.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
India's northeast is connected to the rest of the country by a corridor twenty kilometres wide, and it feels like a different place entirely — greener, quieter, culturally distinct, and visited by a tiny fraction of the travellers who go to Rajasthan or Kerala.

It is also logistically demanding. Distances are long, roads are slow, permits are required for some states, and the weather can genuinely stop you. Plan it properly and it is among the most rewarding trips in India.

## When to Go

- **October to April** — the dry season, and the right window for a first trip
- **October and November** — arguably the best. Post-monsoon greenery, clear skies, comfortable temperatures
- **February to April** — warm, dry, and good for wildlife as water sources concentrate
- **May to September** — the monsoon, and it is a serious one. Meghalaya's Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are among the wettest inhabited places on earth. Roads wash out, landslides close routes, and Kaziranga closes entirely from roughly mid-May to October
- **The exception** — the waterfalls and living root bridges are at their most spectacular in the rain, if you are prepared to be wet and flexible

![Northeast India travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1760462569032-bcc625d06beb?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Meghalaya

The most visited part of the northeast and the best introduction.

**Shillong** — the state capital, a former hill station with a strong music culture and a useful base. Pleasant rather than remarkable; do not linger.

**Cherrapunji (Sohra) and Mawsynram** — the wettest places on earth, on a plateau edge with waterfalls dropping into Bangladesh. **Nohkalikai Falls** is the headline.

**The living root bridges** — the region's signature sight, and genuinely extraordinary. Ficus roots trained across streams over decades until they form a living structure, still growing.

- **The Double Decker at Nongriat** — around 3,000 steps down and the same back up. It is a hard walk and worth every step. **Stay overnight in Nongriat** rather than doing it as a day trip; the village is lovely and the climb back up in the afternoon heat is brutal
- **Mawlynnong** — billed as Asia's cleanest village, with an easier single-decker bridge nearby. Touristed but pleasant
- **Riwai** — an accessible root bridge near Mawlynnong

**Dawki and the Umngot River** — water so clear that boats appear to float above the riverbed. Best November to March; the river is silty after rain. Genuinely busy now, so go early in the day.

**Mawphlang Sacred Forest** — an ancient grove protected by local belief, where nothing may be removed. Quietly remarkable.

**Laitlum Canyons** — a viewpoint over a vast green amphitheatre, and usually empty.

## Assam

The valley state, built around the Brahmaputra.

**Kaziranga National Park** — the big draw. Two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos, plus elephants, wild buffalo, swamp deer and a substantial tiger population. Jeep and elephant safaris across several ranges. **Open roughly November to April**, closed in the monsoon.

Kaziranga is among the most reliable wildlife destinations in India for sightings — the grassland is open and the rhinos are numerous.

**Majuli** — one of the world's largest river islands, reached by ferry from Jorhat. Neo-Vaishnavite monasteries called satras, mask-making, pottery villages, and a pace of life that is the entire point. Stay in a bamboo cottage and do very little. The island is shrinking to erosion, which lends a certain urgency.

**Kaziranga to Majuli** is a natural pairing, a few hours apart.

**Guwahati** — the gateway city and the region's main airport. Kamakhya Temple, river cruises on the Brahmaputra, and a useful transit point. One night is enough.

**Manas National Park** — quieter than Kaziranga, UNESCO-listed, on the Bhutan border.

![Northeast India travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1760462168198-da6a4a87ee09?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Arunachal Pradesh

The most remote, the most demanding, and the most rewarding for those with time.

**Tawang** — a monastery town at 3,000m, home to India's largest monastery and the second largest in the world. Reached over the **Sela Pass** at 4,170m. The drive from Guwahati takes two full days each way, and the road is difficult. Allow at least six days for Tawang alone.

**Ziro Valley** — the Apatani homeland, a broad valley of rice fields and pine hills. The Ziro Music Festival in September is a genuine draw. More accessible than Tawang.

**Namdapha National Park** — extraordinary biodiversity, minimal infrastructure, and a serious expedition.

**Mechuka and Anini** — remote valleys opening slowly to visitors.

**Permits are mandatory.** Indian nationals need an **Inner Line Permit** (obtainable online); foreign nationals need a **Protected Area Permit**, which generally requires travelling in a group of a specified size through a registered operator. Arrange this well in advance — it is the single most common reason trips to Arunachal fall through.

## Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura

Beyond a first trip, but worth knowing:

- **Nagaland** — the **Hornbill Festival** in the first week of December is the region's biggest cultural event, and Kohima's war cemetery is moving
- **Mizoram** — hills, a strong Christian culture, and very few visitors
- **Tripura** — Ujjayanta Palace and the rock carvings at Unakoti
- **Manipur** — Loktak Lake and its floating islands. **Check current advisories carefully** before planning travel here

## A Two-Week Itinerary

- **Day 1** — arrive Guwahati
- **Days 2–5** — Meghalaya: Shillong, Cherrapunji, Nongriat overnight, Mawlynnong and Dawki
- **Day 6** — back to Guwahati, then on toward Kaziranga
- **Days 7–9** — Kaziranga, two full days of safaris
- **Days 10–12** — Majuli via Jorhat
- **Days 13–14** — Ziro Valley, or back to Guwahati

For Tawang, add at least six days and accept that much of it is driving.

## Practicalities

- **Permits** — Arunachal requires them for everyone; Nagaland and Mizoram require them for foreign nationals. Meghalaya and Assam do not. Sort this first
- **Transport** — hire a car and driver. Public transport exists but is slow, and the distances make self-driving a poor idea on unfamiliar mountain roads
- **Distances are deceptive.** A 200km journey can take eight hours. Look at travel times, never at map distance
- **Cash** — essential. ATMs are unreliable outside main towns
- **Connectivity** — patchy. Certain networks work considerably better than others in the hills
- **Accommodation** — homestays and guesthouses rather than hotels outside the main towns, and this is a feature rather than a limitation
- **Costs** — budget $30–45 a day, mid-range $60–100, with the car and driver as the largest single line item

## Why Go

Because it is one of the few places left in India where you can walk to a significant sight and find nobody else there. Because the living root bridges are unlike anything else on earth. Because Kaziranga delivers wildlife sightings that most parks cannot. And because the hospitality in the northeast — in Meghalaya's villages, on Majuli, in Arunachal — is the thing people talk about long after they have forgotten the itinerary.

The permits and the driving times are what make or break this trip, and both need settling before anything is booked. Laying the route out with the real travel times rather than the map distances is the single most useful planning step — **Trypinn** makes those driving days visible, which is exactly where northeast itineraries tend to be over-optimistic.
